front.title: Multicast Dispatch for the Secure Reliable Transport Protocol

abstract.t: This document describes the experimental multicast dispatch profile implemented in Robotweax SRT 0.3.3. One sender transmits shared DATA over IP multicast while maintaining per-receiver unicast control and repair sessions. This initial editorial draft records the wire representation and identifies unresolved protocol and deployment requirements.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: This is an unsubmitted editorial draft. The document name remains provisional. It is not a complete independently implementable specification. Statements describing version 0.3.3 are implementation observations, not IETF consensus. Open issues are intentional and must be resolved or explicitly scoped before claiming conformance.

The baseline is Robotweax SRT commit 69bd5328bf654ebbed894c77fd30ae5b2dfba9d7. This profile uses Live Message Caller/Listener connections. Packet-filter FEC, File/Stream and Rendezvous are excluded. IPv4 multicast has documented sample qualification; an IPv6 encoding is not evidence of IPv6 deployment qualification.

The descriptive sections record the pinned implementation. Recommendations in Open Issues are proposals for review, not approved changes to the existing wire format. Local API states describe this implementation and are not peer-visible protocol fields.

section.name: Transport Model
section.t: The Listener is the sole DATA sender. Each Caller receiver has a unicast session for admission, acknowledgments, negative acknowledgments, key exchange and repairs. Original DATA is emitted once to the multicast destination. Every original and repair names the dispatch group in the DATA destination-socket field, including unicast repairs. The receiver routes both paths into one member reliability state.

Membership uses group type 4, reserved for multicast in the base SRT draft. Use of that value does not imply allocation of the additional handshake extension. The receiver accepts multicast DATA only for the announced group identity and sender source. Source filtering is not cryptographic sender authentication.

Each receiver retains its own control and repair state. The sender remains open without receivers, and accepted sends advance the group position without delivery. The announcement carries the current next-send sequence. Version 0.3.3 emits a timestamp-origin delta of zero: members share the group timestamp origin. The field is serialized and decoded, but no runtime application of a nonzero delta was found in the audited source. Nonzero clock mapping is therefore not specified by this profile. Whether to require zero on reception is an open protocol decision, not a claim about current decoder rejection.

section.name: Admission and Clock Initialization
section.t: For ordinary multicast admission, the Caller selects its inbound sequence from the dispatch announcement before installing the runtime. Native receive membership and ingress routes are attached before the implementation publishes CONNECTED. Attachment failure terminates admission without that publication. An asynchronous connect return indicates work has started; it does not establish successful admission.

The Caller initializes its Live receive-clock base from the local time sampled during runtime attachment minus the peer handshake timestamp. This sample includes setup scheduling delay; it is not a retained UDP-ingress timestamp. Members share receive-clock state within the group. Accepted sender members use the group timestamp origin. The announced timestamp delta is not applied.

Connection publication and group-key confirmation are distinct. CONNECTED and API writable readiness may precede key acknowledgement. Queue acceptance does not promise UDP emission or receiver delivery. Terminal failure can also report writable readiness together with error; applications must inspect the connection state. These API observations do not define additional wire signals.

section.name: Dispatch Handshake Record
section.t: The Listener CONCLUSION carries CONFIG extension type 0x7f14. This provisional value is not an IANA allocation. Content is exactly 60 bytes, excluding the normal four-byte extension header; its length is 15 four-byte words. Integers use network byte order.

Offsets and widths: 0/4 magic 0x52574d01; 4/4 dispatch group ID; 8/1 address family (4 or 6); 9/1 flags; 10/2 destination UDP port; 12/16 multicast address; 28/16 interface selector; 44/4 initial sequence; 48/8 signed timestamp-origin delta in microseconds; 56/1 hop limit; 57/3 reserved zero.

Flag bit 0 indicates an interface hint; other bits are zero. IPv4 addresses occupy the first four bytes of address slots and the remaining bytes are zero. For IPv6, the interface-selector slot contains twelve zero bytes followed by a 32-bit scope index. With no hint, the entire selector is zero. A local receiver interface override takes precedence; an index is host-local and its cross-host meaning remains an open issue.

The implementation rejects wrong length or magic, unknown family/flags, nonzero reserved/padding bytes, a non-multicast destination, port zero, an initial sequence above 0x7fffffff, and invalid group/interface identity. The group ID must have bit 0x40000000 set. This implementation check does not define a global identifier allocation scheme. Duplicate records and unsupported combinations require conformance cases. The timestamp delta is not a validated zero-only reserved field in the current decoder.

section.name: Independent Multicast Source
section.t: Version 0.3.3 adds a bilateral opt-in fixed-source profile. The legacy dispatch record remains exactly 60 bytes. CONFIG type 0x7f15 adds 32 content bytes (eight words), excluding the four-byte extension header, with network-order integers. It is a provisional implementation value, not an allocation.

Offsets and widths are: 0/4 magic 0x52575301; 4/1 kind (1 offer, 2 announcement); 5/1 family (0 offer, 4 IPv4, 6 IPv6); 6/2 source UDP port; 8/4 dispatch group ID; 12/16 source address; 28/4 reserved zero. Offers have zero family, port, group ID and address. IPv4 uses the first four address bytes with twelve zero padding bytes.

The record is restricted to HSv5 CONCLUSION with HSREQ or HSRSP and multicast membership. The Caller offer has no dispatch record. The Listener announcement accompanies the legacy dispatch record and matches its group ID, membership group ID and address family. The source is a concrete non-multicast address with a nonzero port; wildcard, IPv4-mapped IPv6 and scoped wire representations are rejected. Duplicate records, invalid reserved/padding bytes, unsupported magic, invalid context and handshake MTU overflow are rejected. Both peers select the profile; one-sided selection fails with the group rejection reason. Retries preserve the selected source and dispatch snapshot.

The transport uses a dedicated source socket for multicast originals and shared multicast repairs. Control, key exchange and unicast repairs retain the established unicast channel. The C API profile supports IPv4 only, one Listener and one endpoint per receiver; protocol-engine IPv6 encoding is not native IPv6 qualification. Each receiver supplies its own interface selection. Address or port rewriting and automatic source switching are outside this profile.

Multicast DATA is filtered against the negotiated source and dispatch identity before session processing. Route installations carry local generations; stale or replaced bindings cannot update reliability, timing or liveness state. Source filtering is a routing check, not sender authentication. The source record is not covered by session-authentication proofs v2 through v6.

section.name: Delivery and Repairs
section.t: Unicast repair is the default. With a configured threshold of 1 through 16 distinct requesting receivers, a bounded per-sequence tally can cause one multicast repair for shared loss. Suppression begins only after local UDP acceptance. A repeated request by the same receiver uses unicast, permitting recovery if the multicast repair was lost. Transient multicast send failure falls back to unicast.

At each repair decision, the implementation computes a window in microseconds from the requesting member: clamp(2 * smoothed_RTT, 10000, 1000000) when that member has an RTT sample, otherwise 100000. The window is measured from the tally entry first-request time, but recalculated for each requesting member; it is not a fixed shared group RTT. Expiry occurs when elapsed time is strictly greater than this window, or the local clock moves before the recorded first time.

The tally uses 1024 slots indexed by sequence modulo 1024, with at most 16 remembered receiver identities per slot. A repeated receiver request or an unrecordable additional receiver uses unicast. Once an entry has attempted multicast, expiry restores unicast until eviction rather than starting another multicast attempt. Completion is bound to the sequence and attempt identity, preventing stale completion from modifying a replacement entry. These are observed implementation bounds, not yet mandatory limits for independent implementations.

The elected transmitting member must accept a message before suppressed members commit it. In 0.3.3 an ordinary dispatch group with positive group SRTO_MAXBW also has an aggregate unicast-repeat budget, described below. A transient local failure of an original multicast DATA send records submission and relies on receiver NAK recovery; a transient multicast repair failure falls back to the ordinary unicast path. A nontransient send failure breaks the member. Queue acceptance, successful UDP emission and receiver delivery are different events.

section.name: Ordinary Repair Budget and Coordinated Sender
section.t: Ordinary dispatch limits aggregate unicast repeats to four times a positive group SRTO_MAXBW, saturating at the signed 64-bit rate limit. Accounting includes the SRT header and protected payload but excludes IP/UDP headers. Burst credit is the greater of 1500 bytes and 100 milliseconds of that rate and starts empty. Failed UDP submissions spend no credit; a rate change discards accumulated credit. Originals, controls and multicast repairs are excluded. Group values zero or minus one impose no aggregate cap, and changing an individual member does not change the group budget. This is an egress limit, not a congestion-control algorithm, fairness rule or repair-deadline guarantee.

The separate coordinated sender is sender-local and requires independent-source operation and positive SRTO_MAXBW. It uses the same fixed-source wire negotiation. Encoding, original emission, pacing and canonical recovery history are group-owned. Its 64-frame queue accepts one unfragmented Live message per send, with at most 64 members including detached members. Packet filters and session-authentication profiles are refused. Shared multicast repair aggregation is disabled; repairs are canonical unicast DATA. The separate hybrid control context does not turn on a session-authentication profile for DATA membership.

For coordinated sending, SRTO_MAXBW accounts for multicast original DATA including IP/UDP, SRT header and encryption tag. Canonical unicast DATA has a separate aggregate budget of four times that rate, saturating at the unsigned 64-bit limit, with one configured IP MTU of burst credit, initially full. Control and KM traffic are excluded. Failed submissions spend no credit; partial datagram success is fatal and conservatively charged as a full datagram. Hybrid unicast originals, when explicitly enabled, also consume this canonical unicast budget. Ordinary and coordinated byte accounting and burst rules are not interchangeable.

Coordinated readiness reflects group work capacity and key-queue bounds rather than a member flow window. Send success means queue acceptance. Unsubmitted, expired or cancelled originals cannot authorize ACK progress. A stale admission ISN is rejected rather than rebased. With no eligible members the stream advances without emission. If admission detaches the last established members, that send fails without consuming a sequence; subsequent sends can observe an empty group.

Repair-history exhaustion or bounded busy retries can detach a member. Published detachment closes the unicast session, retains a broken group row and sends a single SHUTDOWN; loss of that notification can delay receiver awareness. Rejoining requires reconnect. Hard source failure breaks the group but retains established sessions for inspection and the separately gated source-recovery exception. These local policies do not guarantee remote notification or lossless failover.

section.name: Shared Traffic Keys
section.t: Each receiver has its own key exchange and key-encrypting context, but the sender shares one traffic-key schedule and salt across the dispatch group. Admission requires matching encryption mode and key length. Encrypted group DATA participation requires initial group-key confirmation; admission publication and application queue acceptance can precede that confirmation. A dispatch receiver does not retain the ordinary handshake key clone as an alternate DATA key.

Rotation uses an extended local sequence-position frontier. Generation is floor(position / refresh_rate); the even/odd selector is generation parity. Serial comparison uses the signed distance in the 31-bit sequence space and requires an unambiguous half-range interpretation. Refresh is clamped between 2 and 2^30 positions; preannouncement is at most floor((refresh_rate - 1) / 2). The schedule has four generation-cache slots. This is not a promise of four consecutive populated historical generations after idle jumps.

CTR and GCM use sequence-based IV derivation. A repeated packet reuses its protected representation, with the GCM retransmission bit normalized for AAD. The same key and nonce must not protect different plaintext/header inputs. A complete extended-position/generation algorithm, wrap vectors, key-retention boundary and failure-atomicity rules are still required.

Pending KM requests are retried using the runtime RTT-dependent cadence. Peer-idle expiry measures inactivity since peer activity, independently of the existence of pending key material. This document does not specify a separate maximum KM-completion deadline. Recovery remains subject to configured inactivity limits, queue capacity and packet lifetime.

On a generation-cache miss, the implementation can create a missing key within its retained numeric window, not only the next generation. An idle jump may skip unpopulated generations; generating such a key does not recover a previous cryptogram. Historical repair eligibility must therefore be specified separately from cache capacity. The unused-position advance checks 64-bit overflow before committing its frontier, while the ordinary signed-distance advance does not contain the same explicit check. Complete position-exhaustion semantics remain unresolved.

section.name: Receive-Key Generations in 0.3.3
section.t: The receiver now selects among retained generations using accepted sequence-position ranges and the intervening companion selector. A replacement frontier is a floor for the new generation, not always a ceiling for the retiring one. Delayed old DATA can remain eligible above that frontier until a companion position separates the generations. Eligibility also expires when retirement is at least half the sequence space behind the receive frontier; current keys are not expired by this rule. The rule assumes rotation within half the sequence space.

When position rules leave ambiguity, GCM verifies the policy-selected key first and then only eligible alternatives after an authentication failure; provider errors stop the attempt. Successful authentication identifies the generation and permits accepted-position updates. Failed opens preserve ciphertext and tag even with overlapping output and never publish unauthenticated plaintext. CTR has no such discriminator. While the companion following an observed retired generation is still current, ambiguous routing prefers that retired generation; after the companion also retires, it prefers the newest eligible key. It never inspects plaintext to choose, and an ambiguous choice does not extend accepted ranges. Complete executable retention, missing-companion and rollover vectors remain required for an independent specification.

section.name: Separate Hybrid Control Profile
section.t: Version 0.3.3 also contains default-off hybrid control components requiring explicit ACP1 and HYBRID_CONTROL build options and separate pairwise credentials. They support bounded startup membership recovery, unicast fallback and multicast return. They are scoped in a separate working document rather than added implicitly to the ordinary dispatch protocol. Native handshakes still reject session-authentication version 7; a separate provisional runtime exchange establishes its context.

Explicitly provisioned hybrid startup has a different publication boundary: it stages a unicast dispatch route and waits for authenticated sender-approved unicast policy before publishing CONNECTED. Membership attempts then occur after publication. Unprovisioned public connect still fails on a local multicast join failure. The media sample uses live catch-up and can discard unread media while reporting skipped positions. Fallback is neither lossless nor a decoder-continuity guarantee. The hybrid exchange binds source metadata after the ordinary join; it does not authenticate the announcement at initial admission.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: Shared keys permit admitted receivers to forge traffic authentic under the group key. AES-GCM therefore does not establish sender identity against group insiders; AES-CTR does not provide DATA integrity. Source-address filtering does not fix either limitation.

Leaving does not revoke learned keys; admission does not guarantee that a joiner cannot decrypt retained historical ciphertext protected by its newly learned keys. There is no per-receiver forward/backward access guarantee. Deployments must treat the group as one trusted domain unless a future version supplies stronger protection.

Review must cover handshake tampering, redirection to multicast destinations, unauthorized membership, feedback amplification, receiver state exhaustion, forged control traffic, congestion and denial of service. An implementation source review is not independent cryptographic or network-scale qualification.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: No allocation request is made in this initial editorial version. Types 0x7f14 and 0x7f15 are provisional implementation values; no private-use reservation is asserted. Before publication, coordinate the extension namespace and group-type semantics, decide an allocation policy and specify migration if a collision is found.

section.name: Open Issues
section.t: Proposed compatibility baseline: document the emitted zero timestamp delta and the setup-time receive-clock initialization without silently imposing new receiver rejection or ingress-capture rules. Decide whether a future negotiated profile should change either behavior. Specify complete admission, retry and key-lifecycle state machines, serial arithmetic, position exhaustion, historical repair eligibility and key-retention boundaries.

The implemented 0.3.3 budgets and member limits narrow the earlier resource gap but do not resolve congestion control, feedback limits, fairness, physical-network scale or interface-hint semantics. Decide which limits belong in the interoperable profile and complete its extension-combination matrix. Decide whether a separate pending-key deadline is required. These policy choices remain proposals; the current implementation bounds do not automatically become protocol requirements.

Extend validation where a proposed requirement needs evidence: independent post-rotation DATA vectors, exhaustive lifetime/replay boundaries, independent peer interoperability and physical-network qualification. Existing vectors and local tests do not remove the need for independent security review.

section.name: Source Baseline
section.t: The base protocol is described in . Implementation behavior is taken from . These are informative references in this incomplete editorial version; the normative dependency classification is an open editorial task.

section.name: Implementation Evidence
section.t: The local evidence package includes frozen codec/authentication vectors, six CTR/GCM key-size calculations, serialized handshake/runtime checks and 28 instrumented native loopback scenarios. It distinguishes source-confirmed behavior, executed assertions and unresolved requirements. Logs, hashes, failure explanations and reproduction details are retained outside this protocol text.

The native scenarios cover synchronous/asynchronous admission, join failure, controlled KM loss, bounded queue pressure, selected receive/epoll close schedules, recovery and peer-idle expiry. They support the behavior described here within those fixtures, not independent interoperability, arbitrary deadline guarantees, race freedom or physical-network scale. The release source is unchanged; the native probe uses a separately instrumented export.

The execution results summarized above belong to the earlier 0.3.2 audit, whose annotated tag object is 235cbdb6c0b0d1950b3e74d623ffc21108bf3ef1 and peeled commit is e45d0edd346e5c427d85e4c3b1ac605c81a23397. They were not rerun against 0.3.3 for this editorial update. The 0.3.3 delta is source-reviewed separately; release qualification reports are upstream evidence, not new independent execution.
